edits.draft: Their doubts were not unjustified: the bridge needed major repairs, was declared inadequate in 1890, and it would be 133 years before another suspension bridge was built for railway traffic.
edits.m8-r3: Their doubts were not unjustified: the bridge needed substantial repairs in 1877 and 1880, and it was declared inadequate in 1890.
edits.why: owner's editorial review of 2026-11-04, item 1: the Williamsburg Bridge (1903) carried rail on its suspension deck (NYC DOT), so the report's '133 years' needs a restriction the source does not give; NOTE '133 years later' removed

edits.draft: Beam and arch bridges of steel or reinforced concrete were limited to spans of about 200 to 300 feet.
edits.m8-r3: Wide rivers like the Ohio and the Mississippi, and deep gorges like the one at Niagara, needed bridges that could reach farther.
edits.why: owner's editorial review of 2026-11-04, item 2: the 200-300 ft limit had no period or conditions and contradicts the 1,800 ft arches of C10 (and the Eads Bridge, 1874, 520 ft); replaced by the source's own examples (CLM_752)

edits.draft: In steel, a federal handbook puts plate girders at about 90 to over 500 feet, simple trusses at up to about 750, and cantilever trusses considerably farther. / Arches have spanned from about 200 to 1,800 feet, and cable-stayed bridges from under 200 to nearly 3,000.
edits.m8-r3: A 2012 federal handbook for steel bridges gives two kinds of numbers. / Some are practical ranges: ... / Others are spans that have actually been built: ...
edits.why: owner's editorial review of 2026-11-04, item 3: the card mixed practical/economic ranges with spans built and called all of them 'economic ranges'; the narration and the card now keep the two kinds apart (outlined vs solid bars)

edits.draft: ... and since 1980 almost every American bridge with a main span over 1,000 feet has been cable-stayed.
edits.m8-r3: ... and a 2012 federal handbook found that almost every American bridge built since 1980 with a main span over 1,000 feet was cable-stayed.
edits.why: owner's editorial review of 2026-11-04, item 4: a 2012 statistic, now dated

edits.draft: Today, the long-span answer in America is usually cable-stayed.
edits.m8-r3: In Maine, a modern cable-stayed bridge went up remarkably fast.
edits.why: owner's editorial review of 2026-11-04, item 4: the present-tense claim dropped the conditions of CLM_774 (built in the U.S., main span over 1,000 ft, as of 2012)

edits.draft: Timber beam bridges are still built today, ... / And the most common steel bridge today is still a kind of beam: the welded plate girder.
edits.m8-r3: Timber beam bridges were still being built long after timber trusses, ... / And in 2012, a federal handbook still named a kind of beam, the welded plate girder, as the most common steel bridge.
edits.why: owner's editorial review of 2026-11-04, item 4: 2005 and 2012 statements, now dated (card text too)

edits.draft: Cable-stayed bridges are becoming more common worldwide, and one significant reason is that the methods for erecting them are now better understood.
edits.m8-r3: By 2012, cable-stayed bridges were becoming more common worldwide, and one significant reason was that the methods for erecting them had become better understood.
edits.why: owner's editorial review of 2026-11-04, item 4: a 2012 statement, now dated

edits.draft: ... long after timber trusses fell out of use, and why they are still built on quiet rural roads and in parks today.
edits.m8-r3: ... long after timber trusses stopped being competitive, and in 2005 a national report found them still being built on quiet rural roads and in parks.
edits.why: owner's editorial review of 2026-11-04, item 4: a 2005 statement, now dated; 'fell out of use' was stronger than the source ('ceased to be competitive')

edits.draft: ... suspension and cable-stayed bridges now rely on high-strength steel cables.
edits.m8-r3: ... suspension and cable-stayed bridges came to rely on high-strength steel cables.
edits.why: same review, item 4 (present tense)

edits.draft: Cantilevers had an advantage on uncertain ground. / Unstable soil troubled many foundations, and if a pier sank, a cantilever could adjust, where a continuous beam might fail.
edits.m8-r3: A cantilever like this one is a continuous girder with hinges built in, which made its forces easy to calculate. / So on unstable soil, if a pier sank, its superstructure could adjust, where a continuous beam might build up hidden stresses and fail.
edits.why: owner's editorial review of 2026-11-04, item 5: the source attributes the advantage to the hinged, statically determinate form and to the superstructure

edits.draft: Suspension: cables anchored in massive blocks, set into rock
edits.m8-r3: Suspension: cables anchored in massive blocks or in bedrock (one bank each); cable-stayed foundations drawn in the earth, rock deep
edits.why: owner's editorial review of 2026-11-04, item 6: the card said 'and' where the narration and CLM_761 say 'or'
